subsection.title: Springs and Hooke's law
subsection.p: A spring gives the first natural example of a variable force.

When a spring is at its natural length, it does not need any force to hold it there. When it is stretched, it pulls back. For many springs, at ordinary stretches, the force needed to hold the spring stretched x units is proportional to x:
The constant k is called the spring constant. This relation is called Hooke's law.
A stiffer spring has a larger k. It takes more force to stretch it the same distance.

statement.p: The same spring is already stretched 0.20 meters. How much additional work is required to stretch it to 0.50 meters beyond its natural length?
Stretching from 0.20 to 0.50 meters takes more work than stretching from 0 to 0.20, because the spring is already pulling harder.

warning.p: In Hooke's law, x is the extension from the natural length, not necessarily the total length of the spring.
If a spring has natural length 10 cm and is stretched to length 18 cm, then the extension is 8 cm, not 18 cm.

subsection.title: Energy stored by work
subsection.p: Work transfers energy.

When we stretch a spring, the work we do is stored as elastic potential energy. When we lift a chain, the work becomes gravitational potential energy. When we pump water up and out of a tank, the work raises the water.
This is why work appears so often in physics and engineering. A force acting through a distance can change the energy of a system.
